The program reads all input via getContents, splits into words (whitespace-separated tokens), first token is integer T, then take T strings and for each check if valid parentheses string, print YES/NO. Need preserve behavior for all valid inputs: strings consist only of '(' and ')'? The specification says 소괄호 문자열, likely only '(' and ')', but the Haskell code also checks c == '(' and c == ')' and otherwise False, so it handles any character but rejects non-parens. We should mimic: if any character not '(' or ')', isValid returns False. The program uses `words`, which splits on whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines), so input format is T then each string separated by whitespace, no whitespace within string. The example shows each string on separate line but could be spaces. words handles that. In C++, we should read all input similarly: first token T, then next T tokens, each token is a string of parentheses, possibly with other characters? But spec says only parentheses. We'll implement using cin >> T then loop reading strings via cin >> s. That's equivalent to words for standard whitespace-separated input. In case there are fewer tokens than T? Haskell take t rest will take as many as available, if fewer, it will process fewer, no error. In C++, we can read T, then loop for i from 0..T-1 and read a string, but if input ends early, the extraction will fail and we break? However, for valid inputs, T matches number of strings, but we should handle gracefully. We can use while (T-- && cin >> s) to process available strings. That matches take t rest: if fewer tokens, process available. If more tokens? After processing T, ignores rest. So while (T-- > 0 && cin >> s). But note order: we need read T first. In Haskell, if tStr missing, returns. In C++, if first token missing, we can just exit. So implement: int T; if (!(cin >> T)) return 0; string s; while (T-- > 0 && cin >> s) { ... }. But careful: order of T-- and reading s: while condition checks T-- > 0 first, then reads s? In C++, comma? Actually while (T-- > 0 && cin >> s) evaluates T-- > 0 first (decrements T), then if true, evaluates cin >> s. That's fine: it will attempt to read for each decremented T. But when T becomes 0, short-circuit doesn't read, but we still decrement? Actually T-- > 0 evaluates using current T then decrements. So initial T=6: first iteration, T-- > 0 true (T becomes 5), then read s. Next iteration T-- > 0 true (T becomes 4), read. When T becomes 0? Let's simulate: initial T=6, iteration 1: condition T-- > 0 => 6>0 true, T becomes5; read. iteration2: 5>0 true, T becomes4; read. iteration3: 4>0 true, T becomes3; read. iteration4: 3>0 true, T becomes2; read. iteration5: 2>0 true, T becomes1; read. iteration6: 1>0 true, T becomes0; read. After sixth read, loop ends. Next check: T-- > 0 => 0>0 false, T becomes -1, exits. So total reads = original T. Good. If input ends early, cin >> s fails and loop stops. Good.

Now implement isValid: given string s, use int bal =0; for char c in s: if c=='(' bal++; else if c==')' { if (bal ==0) return false; bal--; } else return false; after loop return bal==0. That exactly matches Haskell.

Output each result with newline.
